title: A field guide to base R
summary: Read and write the base R you will meet in other people's code: subset vectors and data frames with [, take columns with $ and [[, apply a function to every column, loop with for, and draw quick charts with plot(), hist() and barplot().

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse)

runs.purpose: load the tidyverse, to read the data

steps.explain: This lesson reads the data with readr and does everything else with base R, the functions that come with R itself. Much of the R code you'll find online is written this way.

steps.title: Subsetting vectors: [

runs.purpose: read one week of trips into `week`
take the trips' lengths as a vector, `minutes`
runs.task: Store the `duration_min` column of `week` as a vector called `minutes`, with `$`.

runs.purpose: keep the lengths over an hour
runs.task: Keep the elements of `minutes` greater than 60, with `[` and a condition.

steps.explain: `[` picks elements of a vector: by position, `minutes[1:5]`; leaving some out, `minutes[-1]`; or with a logical vector of the same length, keeping the `TRUE`s, as `minutes[minutes > 60]` does. That is the base R way to filter: {n_long} trips that week lasted over an hour. `filter()` does the same for the rows of a data frame.

steps.title: Data frames: df[rows, columns]

alternatives: week |> filter(member_type == 'casual', duration_min > 60) |> select(start_station, end_station, duration_min)
runs.purpose: keep casual riders' trips of over an hour, and three of their columns
runs.task: With `week[rows, columns]`, keep the rows where `member_type` is "casual" and `duration_min` is over 60, and the columns `start_station`, `end_station` and `duration_min`.

steps.explain: A data frame takes two subscripts, `[rows, columns]`. Rows here are picked by a condition, and columns by name. Inside `[`, columns must be written as `week$member_type`, since base R doesn't look names up in the data the way dplyr does. Leave a subscript empty to keep everything: `week[, "bike_type"]` keeps all rows. The same result in dplyr is `filter()` then `select()`, and this step's check accepts either.

steps.title: One column: $ and [[

runs.purpose: count the trips on each kind of bike, taking the column with [[
runs.task: Count the values of the `bike_type` column with `table()`, taking the column with `week[["bike_type"]]`.

runs.purpose: print the mean of two columns, naming each column in a variable
runs.task: Loop over `c("distance_km", "duration_min")` with `for`, and for each `column` print its name and `mean(week[[column]])` with `cat()`, ending with `"\n"`.

steps.explain: `$` and `[[` both take one column out of a data frame as a vector. `$` needs the name written out, `week$bike_type`; `[[` takes a string, so the name can be in a variable, which is what the loop needs. A `for` loop runs its body once for each element: `column` is "distance_km", then "duration_min". `cat()` prints without quotes or `[1]`, and `"\n"` starts a new line. In the tidyverse, `across()` usually does the same job without a loop.

steps.title: A function for every column: vapply() and lapply()

runs.purpose: ask of every column whether it holds numbers
runs.task: Ask whether each column of `week` is numeric, with `vapply(week, is.numeric, logical(1))`.

runs.purpose: split the lengths by rider type and find each group's median
runs.task: Split `week$duration_min` by `week$member_type` with `split()`, then find each part's median with `lapply()`.

steps.explain: A data frame is a list of columns, so `vapply()` can call a function on each column: {n_numeric} of them are numeric. `logical(1)` promises one `TRUE` or `FALSE` from each, and `vapply()` stops if that's broken. `lapply()` returns a list, with no promise to keep. `split()` cuts a vector into a list of groups, so `lapply()` on it summarises each group: base R's `summarize(.by = )`. `map()` from purrr is the tidyverse's `lapply()`.

steps.title: Quick charts: hist(), plot() and barplot()

runs.purpose: draw a histogram of trip lengths
runs.task: Draw a histogram of `week$duration_min` with `hist()` and `breaks = 40`.

runs.purpose: plot each trip's length against its distance
draw a bar for each kind of bike
runs.task: Draw a bar chart of the counts in `table(week$bike_type)` with `barplot()`.

steps.explain: Base R's charts take vectors rather than a data frame and mappings, and draw straight away. `hist()` cuts the lengths into bins, about 40 of them here; `plot()` of two numeric vectors draws a scatter plot, x first; `barplot()` draws the counts from `table()`. They are quick for a first look, and you'll see them in older code and help pages, but ggplot2's layers, legends and facets take far less work for a finished chart.
